passages.t: Bones under the stars, and the stork knows her time
passages.happening:
The LORD says that the bones of Judah's kings, officials, priests, prophets and people will be taken from their graves (verse 1). ‘They will be exposed to the sun and moon, and to all the host of heaven which they have loved, served, followed, consulted, and worshiped’ (verse 2). They will lie unburied, like dung on the ground. The survivors will choose death over life (verse 3).

‘Do men fall and not get up again? Does one turn away and not return?’ (verse 4). Why then does Jerusalem always turn away and refuse to return (verse 5)? No one repents or asks what he has done. Each charges on his own course ‘like a horse charging into battle’ (verse 6). ‘Even the stork in the sky knows her appointed seasons’ (verse 7), and the dove, the swift and the thrush keep their times, ‘but My people do not know the requirements of the LORD’ (verse 7).

They claim to be wise and to have the law, but ‘the lying pen of the scribes has produced a deception’ (verse 8). They have rejected the word of the LORD, so what wisdom do they have (verse 9)? From the least to the greatest all are greedy for gain, and the prophets and priests still dress the wound lightly and promise peace (verses 10 and 11).
passages.hearers:
Burial mattered deeply in Israel. To be buried with one's ancestors was a last dignity, and to lie unburied was the worst curse the law named. The leaders will be laid out before the very sun, moon and stars they worshiped, and those gods will do nothing for them. King Manasseh had promoted the worship of the stars, and though Josiah removed it, it had plainly survived.

The land lies on one of the world's great bird migration routes, along the Jordan Valley between Africa and the north. Every spring and autumn huge flocks of storks and other birds pass over. Jeremiah's hearers watched them come and go on time. The birds follow the order God built into creation. God's people do not follow his.

The lying pen of the scribes may mean those who wrote and taught the law but twisted it to suit themselves. Having the law on scrolls did not make anyone wise if they would not hear the word of the LORD.
passages.later: The law named the curse of the unburied: ‘Your corpses will be food for all the birds of the air’ (Deuteronomy 28:26). Isaiah made the same comparison with the animals: ‘The ox knows its owner’ (Isaiah 1:3).
passages.asks: The stork knows her season, and God's people do not know his ways. Ask what rhythms of God's word you have ignored that are as plain as the seasons. And ask whether your knowledge of Scripture has made you wiser, or only surer of yourself.

passages.t: The harvest is past, and no balm in Gilead
passages.happening:
God will take away the harvest. There will be no grapes on the vine or figs on the tree, and even the leaves will wither (verse 13).

The people say to one another that they should flee to the walled towns and die there, for the LORD has given them poisoned water to drink (verse 14). ‘We hoped for peace, but no good has come, for a time of healing, but there was only terror’ (verse 15). The snorting of the enemy's horses is heard from Dan, and the whole land shakes (verse 16). God will send snakes that cannot be charmed (verse 17).

Then the prophet's grief. ‘My sorrow is beyond healing; my heart is faint within me’ (verse 18). He hears his people crying from a far land, asking if the LORD is no longer in Zion (verse 19). ‘The harvest has passed, the summer has ended, but we have not been saved’ (verse 20). ‘For the brokenness of the daughter of my people I am crushed’ (verse 21). ‘Is there no balm in Gilead? Is no physician there? Why then has the health of the daughter of my people not been restored?’ (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
Verse 20 draws on the farming year. The grain harvest came in spring and the fruit in late summer. If both had passed and the storehouses were still empty, there was nothing left to hope for until next year. The people had waited through every season for rescue, and none came.

Dan was the northernmost town of the land, so the horses heard from Dan are the invader at the border.

Gilead, the hill country east of the Jordan, was known for its balm, a fragrant resin used as medicine and traded widely. The traders who bought Joseph were carrying balm from Gilead to Egypt. Jeremiah asks why, with the medicine so close, his people are not healed. The answer, through the whole book, is that they would not come to be healed.
passages.later: Joseph was sold to a caravan from Gilead carrying ‘spices, balm, and myrrh’ (Genesis 37:25). Lamentations, written after the fall, cries in the same voice: ‘My eyes fail from weeping’ (Lamentations 2:11).
passages.hard:
Who is weeping in verses 18 to 22, Jeremiah or God?

Most readers hear Jeremiah, and the chapter supports that: he hears the people's cry from a far land. Yet the lines are broken in verse 19 by God's own question about why they provoked him, and in verse 11 God himself speaks of the daughter of his people. Some interpreters therefore hear God grieving through the prophet's voice, or the prophet's grief so fully sharing God's that the two cannot be separated.

Readers who hold that God does not suffer as people do, and readers who stress God's real involvement, can agree on this: judgment here is not delivered in cold anger. Whether the tears are the prophet's, God's or both, the one who judges is not indifferent.

Grief is not a lack of faith. If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The people said the harvest had passed and they were not saved. Ask whether you have waited through seasons for a help that did not come, and what you did with that. And ask who around you is wounded and near the balm, but has not yet been healed.
